content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers a poisoning scenario of availability attacks, where the protectors (who implement poisoning attacks) release the perturbed training data, so that the hacker (who train models on the poisoned data) cannot achieve high test accuracy. 

Unlike previous work that requires the knowledge of class labels in advance, this paper assumes that hackers and protectors have different labels for the same image (i.e., the *label-inconsistency* scenario). In the proposed scenario, the authors experimentally find that previous attack methods are no longer effective. Then, the authors propose a new method called UniversalCP, and empirically verify that it is an effective availability attack without knowing the label information.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- This paper outlines a practical scenario for availability attacks called label-inconsistency, which allows protectors and hackers to hold different labels for the same image. This scenario would broaden the applicability of availability attacks.

- A new attack method called UniversalCP is proposed to achieve better attack performance in the *label-inconsistency* scenario.

Weaknesses:

- This paper is mainly an empirical study. However, the basic experimental setup in the paper is not only not faithful to the *label-consistency* scenario, but also an incomplete demonstration of the *label-inconsistency* scenario.
  - In the *label-consistency* scenario, as the authors have realized, the labels used for the same image to train the surrogate model and the victim model are identical. Therefore, to identify the impact of label-inconsistency, only the labels should be changed, while keeping the training images unchanged. However, for example, in Section 3 (Problem Statement), the authors change both the images used to train the surrogate model and the labels used to generate poisons (i.e., unlearnable examples). Since the images used to train the surrogate model and the victim model are not the same, it is hard to conclude that the current SOTA attacks are inefficient due to label inconsistency. After all, their failures may come from the change in the distribution of the images. In this regard, the conclusion in Section 3.2 is misleading. Similar pitfalls exist in other experiments in this paper.
  - Although one ignores the pitfalls of different training images, the particular setup described in Section 3.1 is still incomplete. Specifically, the authors only consider one case where the number of classes used to train the surrogate model $\|\Omega\|$ is much larger than the number of the classes used to train the victim model $\|\mathcal{Y}\|$, i.e., $\|\Omega\| \gg \|\mathcal{Y}\|$. However, evidently, there exist other realistic cases such as 1) $\|\Omega\| \ll \|\mathcal{Y}\|$ and 2) $\|\Omega\| = \|\mathcal{Y}\|$ but $\Omega \neq \mathcal{Y}$. Therefore, the particular case of $\|\Omega\| \gg \|\mathcal{Y}\|$ considered in this paper is limited and cannot completely represent the *label-inconsistency* scenario.

- Adversarial training should be considered as a defense against the proposed poisoning method. Since recent works have shown that the damage of many perturbation-based availability attacks can be largely mitigated by adversarial training, it is inadvisable to disregard the defense ability of adversarial training.

- The authors claim that "it is paranoid to consider adversarial training as a potential defense", because the computational cost of adversarial training is "very expensive" and "one or two order of magnitude higher than normal training". Such claims might be justifiable in 2017, but become conservative in 2022. After years of improvement, adversarial training can actually be a fast and efficient defense. Nowadays, one can implement "adversarial training for free", and even more, it is well-known that "fast is better than free". Therefore, adversarial training currently is very practical in applications where many clean instances and/or labels are expensive.

- A very simple modification of existing methods should be considered to adapt them to the experimental setup of this paper. For example, in Section 3, the authors adopt ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet-1k as the surrogate model, while the victim's task is CIFAR-10. This setup creates a very large gap in the number of classes, resulting in the failures of the existing methods. Thus, a simple modification is to restrict the number of classes used by the protectors during generating poisons (i.e., make the protectors only use 10 labels). In other words, the specific target labels (and specific cluster centers) for adversarial poisoning or error-minimizing noise may need not be precise/correct. What matters would be the number of target labels (and specific cluster centers). In summary, the authors should consider this simple modification; otherwise, the setup is very unfair to the existing methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- There are several typos. E.g., "Through feeding the it into K-means algorithm" in Section 4.2.
- The notations in Section 3.1 are a little complicated.
- The proposed method called UniversalCP is incremental.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a practical scenario called *label-inconsistency*, which is more flexible than the existing *label-consistency* scenario. However, though this paper is mainly experimental, the empirical study is insufficient to demonstrate the proposed scenario and the proposed method. On one hand, the basic experimental setup is unfaithful and incomplete, so the conclusions would be misleading. On the other hand, the proposed attack method lacks performance evaluation under adversarial training, a popular defense against perturbation-based availability attacks, and lacks a fair comparison with a simple modification of the existing methods.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The poisoning attack is the main focus of this paper. The authors state that the label-consistency assumption will fail in many cases, and claim a new scenario named label inconsistency. The label-inconsistent scenario allows the hacker and the protector to consider different label space, which is more practical but also more challenging. Inspired by their finding of uniformity and discrepancy (in label consistency), the authors propose a novel method called UniversalCP, which generates the universal unlearnable examples by cluster-wise perturbation. The authors verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods under a variety of experimental settings with various backbones, datasets, and commercial applications. The authors claim the superiority of their methods against advanced counterparts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
> Strengths

- *The novelty of this paper lies in introducing a new attack scenario named label inconsistency*. In general, the authors state that previous assumption on label consistency is unrealistic, considering the situations where the hacker and the protector consider the same label space. However, in reality, the protector only releases unlabeled images to the hacker via the web, and the hacker cannot know the label space considered by the hacker. Therefore, the authors suggest the label inconsistent assumption, which assume the labels owned by the protector and the labels owned by the hacker are inconsistent. Moreover, the authors found that the current methods suffer from a significant reduction in effectiveness for the label-inconsistent situations, making the considered problem a challenging but attractive one. 

- *The authors conduct extensive experiments on various datasets with various backbone models*. The authors carry out their study on 6 high-resolution and industrial-scale vision datasets. The authors adopt a series of deep models including RN-18, RN-50, ViT, EN1, RNX1.6, among many others. The authors try hard to demonstrate the effectiveness of their methods against representative baseline methods, ablation study and further experiments are also very interesting to me. 

> Weaknesses

- *It is unclear why the observations in the label-consistent scenario can also hold for label inconsistency*. The authors test two representative methods in the label-consistent scenario, and find their success lies in that they disrupt the uniformity and discrepancy of data distribution in feature representation. Inspired by this, the authors introduce their UniversalCP for the label inconsistent situation. However, I am not sure why the conclusion in the label consistent scenario can be generalized to the case of label inconsistency, since the latter is actually a new attack scenario. 

- *The comparison in experiments may be unfair*. The authors adopted CLIP as the surrogate models to generate unlearnable examples, which enjoys strong representation capabilities and large semantic supervision. However, the baseline methods do not adopt the similar surrogate models, which may make the experimental results unconvincing.  Especially, I am not if the improved experimental results are benefit from more complex surrogate models or the proposed UniversalCP. 

- *The proposed method requires detailed discussion*. As claimed, the proposed method (Eq. 1 to be specified) is motivated by the observation in the label consistent cases, i.e., disrupting the uniformity and the discrepancy of the embedding features. However, detailed discussion about why the proposed method can disrupting the uniformity and the discrepancy is missing, which may make the proposed method not very convincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, the paper is clearly written and is easy to follow. To me, the motivation is a little bit of unclear. Especially, I cannot fully understand 1) why the conclusion of uniformity and discrepancy studied in the label-consistent case can be generalized to the label-inconsistent case; and 2) why the proposed learning objective in Eq. 1 leads to the considered uniformity and discrepancy. From my opinion, addressing these two issues can be helpful in improving the quality of the paper. Besides, I did not check the reproducibility of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper considers a new attack scenario in poisoning attacks, which is pretty convincing to me. To improve the quality of the paper, it will be great if the authors could address my concerns in the Summary of the Paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper identified the challenges when applying unlearnable examples in real-world settings. The protector and model trainer could use different labels for the different objects (with a similar semantic concept), which is not studied in previous works. This paper proposed a cluster-wise perturbation to generate unlearnable examples. Results show it can outperform existing works if the protector and model trainer does not use the same labeling scheme. The proposed method also demonstrates its effectiveness on commercial platforms such as Azure and PaddlePaddle.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
- The label consistency/inconsistency identified in this paper is very interesting and ignored in existing works. Label-inconsistency setting should greatly improve the feasibility of unlearnable examples in real-world scenarios. 
- The proposed method is simple but non-trivial. 
- The empirical results validated the proposed method, appreciated for validating the results on commercial platforms.


Weaknesses
- Disrupting the uniformity and discrepancy is an empirical observation rather than theoretically proven. This part could cause confusion in Section 4.1. 
- It would be nice to add UnivsersalCP/UnivsersalCP-CLIP to Figure 2 to demonstrate the proposed method can actually achieve disrupting the uniformity and discrepancy at the same time since this is one of the main motivations for the proposed method. 
- Section 3.1, threat model, social media companies could also use users' data for training commercial models. Perhaps another example is more suitable. 
- For generating UnivsersalCP, does the protector have access to the entire dataset? In order to generate CP, it has to be able to generate the clusters. It seems like the protector has to have access to all the data. If so, this method is suitable for companies to protect their data rather than for individual users. This part is unclear in the paper.
- What happens if the surrogate model (classifier) is trained on fewer classes than the victim model in the label inconsistency setting (
$\overline m < m$)? 
- The cluster-wise perturbation applies the same noise to every sample that belongs within this cluster. This could be detected, as shown by Yu et al., 2022. The adaptive case should be examined. What if the model trainer is aware of Universal-CP? How much effort is needed to detect samples with Universal-CP or even reverse/remove the noise? This should be carefully examined. See the reasons listed in [1].

[1] Data Poisoning Won't Save You From Facial Recognition, ICLR 2022
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: few statements/points is unclear. Other parts are easy to follow.

Quality: good

Novelty: good

Reproducibility: no open-source code was provided, but based on the description of the paper, it should be easily reproduced. It would be great if additional details were provided regards of Section 5.3.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the merit outweighted the weakness of this paper. Label inconsistency is indeed an area that needs to be studied. The effectiveness evaluated on the commercial platform shows practicality. The main weakness is that the cluster-wise noise, if one of them is leaked, might invalidate all others. Also, the use case/settings could be more clear.

content.title: Universal Unlearnable Examples: Cluster-wise Perturbations without Label-consistency
content.abstract: There is a growing interest in employing unlearnable examples against privacy leaks on the Internet, which prevents the unauthorized models from being properly trained by adding invisible image noise. However, existing attack methods rely on an ideal assumption called label-consistency. In this work, we clarify a more practical scenario called \emph{label-inconsistency} that allows hackers and protectors to hold different labels for the same image. Inspired by disrupting the \emph{uniformity} and \emph{discrepancy}, we present a novel method called \emph{UniversalCP} on label-inconsistency scenario, which generates the universal unlearnable examples by cluster-wise perturbation. Furthermore, we investigate a new strategy for selecting the CLIP as the surrogate model, since vision-and-language pre-training models are trained on large-scale data and more semantic supervised information. We also verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods and the strategy for selecting surrogate models under a variety of experimental settings including black-box backbones, datasets and even commercial platforms Microsoft {\tt Azure} and Baidu {\tt PaddlePaddle}.
